content.title: Official Review for DC-VAE
content.review:
This paper proposed to replace the ELBO loss in VAE-GAN with an instance-level contrastive loss to improve the performance of image synthesis and reconstruction. Experiments on multiple benchmarks of images demonstrate the effectiveness of DC-VAE on image synthesis and reconstruction, and latent representation learning.

Strengths:
The improvements of DC-VAE on the benchmarks over VAE-GAN and other baselines are impressive.

Weakness:
1. The motivation of replacing the ELBO loss with the contrastive loss is not clearly introduced. Both the two losses work for the instance-level fidelity. Why the contrastive loss is better than the BLBO loss? 

2. The paper is not clearly written, some parts are confusing. For example, what is Theorem 1 telling us? I cannot understand it. Moreover, how to optimize the contrastive loss (6) in practice? 

Other comments and questions:

1. Some notations are inconsistent. For example, in Eq (3), F_l() is denoted as the l-th layer feature embedding of D. But in Eq (6), D_l() is used. These inconsistent notations make the paper more difficult to be understood.

2. In the first sentence of introduction, I cannot understand the three types of representation learning divided by the authors. Why CNNs are categorized as encoders and Transformers as autoencoders? 

3. In the last two sentences in the second paragraph, the authors claim "once an encoder and a decoder are joined together, the reconstruction/synthesis of the decoder often becomes degenerated." I don't believe that it is the joint learning of encoder and decoder leads to degenerated decoder. And what is the relation of this sentence with the following one "Note that Transformers, consisting of both encoder and decoder, are trained for temporal data with sequence-to-sequence prediction." I cannot follow what the two sentences want to say.

Overall, the contrastive loss proposed in this paper is interesting, and the experimental results are impressive. However, the paper is not ready to be published and needs to be revised fundamentally.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: We thank reviewer 2 for the valuable feedback. Please find our reply to the questions below.
content.comment:
Q1. "The motivation of replacing the ELBO loss with the contrastive loss is not clearly introduced. Both the two losses work for the instance-level fidelity. Why the contrastive loss is better than the ELBO loss?

A1. To simplify the notation, we show the difference between reconstruction and contrastive loss based on the input $x$ and it's reconstruction $f_{\theta}(z)$ (in the paper, output layer feature $F_D(x)$ for the CNN is used for the measurement).
As explained in the paper (section 4.1), the reconstruction loss enforces the similarity between the reconstructed image and the input image $\min ||x-f_{\theta}(z)||$  while the GAN loss computes an adversarial loss $\min \max_{w} \log (\frac{1}{1+\exp(-w \cdot x)}) + \log (1-\frac{1}{1+\exp(-w \cdot f_{\theta}(z))})$. The reconstruction loss term enforces pixel/feature matching while the GAN loss encourages the reconstruction and input discriminatively non-separable; the two are measured in different ways resulting in a conflict. Our contrastive loss on the other hand, is also a discriminative term, it can be viewed as $\min -\log \frac{\exp\{(x \cdot f_{\theta}(z))\}}{\sum_{j=1}^n \exp\{(x_j \cdot  f_{\theta}(z))\}}$. To compare the reconstruction loss with the contrastive loss: the former wants to have an exact match between the reconstruction with the input, whereas the later is more relaxed to be ok if no exact match but as the closest one amongst all the training samples.

In other words, the reconstruction wants a perfect match for the instance-level fidelity whereas the contrastive loss is asking for being the most similar one among the given training samples. Using the contrastive loss gives more room and creates less conflict with the GAN loss.

Q2. "The paper is not clearly written, some parts are confusing. For example, what is Theorem 1 telling us? I cannot understand it. Moreover, how to optimize the contrastive loss (6) in practice?"

A2. Theorem 1 is justifying that our proposed IELBO implicitly estimates the log likelihood required for ELBO, and thus we can replace ELBO with IELBO. To optimize the contrastive loss, we follow the same method as in the paper “Momentum Contrast for Unsupervised Visual Representation Learning”, which uses momentum based queues. MOCO has become a widely adopted technique for minimizing the contrastive loss in self-supervised learning: https://github.com/facebookresearch/moco


Q3. "Some notations are inconsistent. For example, in Eq (3), F_l() is denoted as the l-th layer feature embedding of D. But in Eq (6), D_l() is used. These inconsistent notations make the paper more difficult to be understood."

A3. Thank you for pointing it out. We have revised the notation in Eq (3)  to make it consistent with that in Eq (6).


Q4. "In the first sentence of introduction, I cannot understand the three types of representation learning divided by the authors. Why CNNs are categorized as encoders and Transformers as autoencoders?"

A4. A bottom-up convolutional neural network can be considered as an encoder that projects an image to a latent/embedding space. For example, the GAN family adopts standard CNN (image->projected vector) as the encoder. Transformer consists of an encoder and a decoder to perform sequence to sequence learning/translation. We have revised this part of the statement to make it more precise.


Q5. "In the last two sentences in the second paragraph, the authors claim "once an encoder and a decoder are joined together, the reconstruction/synthesis of the decoder often becomes degenerated." I don't believe that it is the joint learning of encoder and decoder leads to degenerated decoder. And what is the relation of this sentence with the following one "Note that Transformers, consisting of both encoder and decoder, are trained for temporal data with sequence-to-sequence prediction." I cannot follow what the two sentences want to say."

A5. Based on the extensive experimental results reported in the deep learning literature, the quality of synthesized images by SOTA GAN models, e.g. ProgressiveGAN and BigGAN, is almost always better than that of the existing SOTA VAE. This is because the extra requirement in VAE to be able to additionally reconstruct the input (encoder+decoder) whereas GAN’s main objective is to generate samples that are faithful to the input data manifold. As explained in the response earlier about the conflict between the reconstruction loss and the GAN loss, having the encoder and decoder architecture introduces an extra demand to VAE, making it a sacrifice in the quality of the output of the decoder.

The statement is to point out that Transformer also consists of an encoder and decoder but it is not in the same sense as the standard VAE type autoencoder. We have deleted the descriptions in the revised version to remove confusions.

content.title: Review: DUAL CONTRADISTINCTIVE GENERATIVE AUTOENCODER
content.review:
Review: DUAL CONTRADISTINCTIVE GENERATIVE AUTOENCODER

Summary: The paper presents a new generative model called DC-VAE which leverages instance-level and set-level constrastive losses together to achieve simultaneously sharp outut images in reconstruction, in sampling and representation learning. The results appear to be similar or better than other comparable approaches like VAE-GAN (Larsen et al. 2016) which in itself improves upon VAE.

##########################################################################

Reasons for score: 

While I appreciate the idea and the results look promising, a closer examination of the results raises several questions.
These questions must be addressed in order for me to raise the score.

##########################################################################

Pros:
- The model is interesting, the idea is well justified, and to my knowledge, this specific combination of ideas is novel, though the building blocks are largely well known.
- The presentation is clear.
- The model is general-purpose and hence potentially with wide range of applications.
- There are indications of good performance.

##########################################################################

Cons:
- The experiments do not seem to form a coherent whole. Some results are only given in qualitative (visual) way which leaves room for heavy cherry-picking (faithfulness or LSUN reconstructions is only indicated in 3 images in fig 1, so are the reconstructions of CIFAR in fig.4, and the IntroVAE comparison). The faithfulness of reconstructions should be quantitatively measured if the authors want it to carry weight.
- Some claims seem to imply that results in very different resolutions are comparable. One cannot make this assumption.
- IntroVAE comparison is problematic. First, IntroVAE paper itself does not even claim that their reconstructions would retain the identity of the face, but only the general topology, and thus they often lose the identity. So it is a problematic comparison point to begin with since the authors do not discuss the identity question at all. Second, the authors compare 128x128 results of their model to 1024x1024 results of IntroVAE, and instead of granting that the capacity to learn a high resolution may cause more loss of details, they make the contrary claim that their model is "already better" at the low resolution. I do not agree with this interpretation. You cannot compare models that have this large of a difference in resolution and draw that kind of a conclusion.
- Smoothness of latent space is not evaluated in any way (e.g. by interpolations)
- Minor: There could be many more comparison points and it is not clear why these exact ones were chosen. E.g. [1-6] seem to be relevant prior work and some of them as potential baselines. Either (Donahue et al., 2018) or (Dumoulin et al., 2018) could also be better contrasted to or used as a baseline.

##########################################################################

Questions during rebuttal period:
- How is the FID of reconstructions computed exactly? Is the reconstructed set of (how many?) samples compared against the set of the original samples?
- What do you mean by using ProgressiveGAN for the 128x128 architecture in 5.1? Do you mean you just use their 128x128 structure in a static manner, and not the progressive growing?
- Can you show also latent interpolations or Perceptual Path Length (Karras et al., 2018) measurements?

[1] A. Makhzani, J. Shlens, N. Jaitly, and I. Goodfellow. Adversarial autoencoders. In International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2016.
[2] L. Mescheder, S. Nowozin, and A. Geiger. Adversarial variational Bayes: Unifying variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. In International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), pages 2391–2400, 2017
[3] A. Heljakka, A. Solin, and J. Kannala. Pioneer networks: Progressively growing generative autoencoder. In Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV), pages 22–38, 2018.
[4] D. Ulyanov, A. Vedaldi, and V. Lempitsky. It takes (only) two: Adversarial generator-encoder networks. In Proceedings of the Thirty-Second AAAI Conference on Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AAAI), pages 1250–1257, 2018.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: We thank reviewer 3 for the constructive comments. Please find our answers to the questions below.
content.comment:
Q1. “The experiments do not seem to form a coherent whole. Some results are only given in qualitative (visual) way which leaves room for heavy cherry-picking (faithfulness or LSUN reconstructions is only indicated in 3 images in fig 1, so are the reconstructions of CIFAR in fig.4, and the IntroVAE comparison). The faithfulness of reconstructions should be quantitatively measured if the authors want it to carry weight.”

A1. The images shown in the original paper and the revised version were not cherry picked.
We have reported faithfully the quantitative measure for the reconstructions in the ablation study. 
Thank you for pointing out that we do not have sufficient reconstruction images. 
We have added a large grid of reconstruction results on LSUN and CelebAHQ datasets in the appendix to address your concern.  As seen in the main body as well as Appendix of the paper, the effectiveness of the proposed method for reconstruction and synthesis is evident.


Q2. “Some claims seem to imply that results in very different resolutions are comparable. One cannot make this assumption.”

A2. Thank you for pointing it out. In the original submission, we obtained trained model for images of size $32 \times 32$, $64 \times 64$, and $128 \times 128$, which are difficult for VAE to have high quality images on. In the revised version, we have updated the CelebA image reconstruction and synthesis with a higher resolution, $512 \times 512$ by following the backbone and training process of ProGAN for CelebA-HQ.


Q3. “IntroVAE comparison is problematic. First, IntroVAE paper itself does not even claim that their reconstructions would retain the identity of the face, but only the general topology, and thus they often lose the identity. So it is a problematic comparison point to begin with since the authors do not discuss the identity question at all. Second, the authors compare 128x128 results of their model to $1024 \times 1024$ results of IntroVAE, and instead of granting that the capacity to learn a high resolution may cause more loss of details, they make the contrary claim that their model is "already better" at the low resolution. I do not agree with this interpretation. You cannot compare models that have this large of a difference in resolution and draw that kind of a conclusion.”

A3. Thank you for raising the issues.
- In terms of the comparison with IntroVAE in reconstruction, we think it is still helpful illustrating the characteristics of the proposed DC-VAE method. These images were shown in the IntroVAE paper [Huang et al. 2018] and the first four out of 6 were selected in the original paper (for the space concern) and we are showing all 6 images in the updated version. Our goal is to show a qualitative comparison with a competitive VAE method for reconstruction in the sense of the overall quality, not particularly about maintaining the identity. Both the reconstructed faces (128x128) in the original paper and the ones (512x512) in the revised version show a clear advantage of DC-VAE over IntroVAE. Since the reconstruction capability for VAE is one of its main properties, comparing the reconstruction quality of VAE models seems to be important.
- We have updated the paper with higher resolution images of size 512x512. The reconstruction further confirms with our findings for the effectiveness of DC-VAE.


Q4. “Smoothness of latent space is not evaluated in any way (e.g. by interpolations)”

A4. Thank you for the suggestion. We have added latent interpolation results on CelebA-HQ, LSUN Bedroom (Figure 5, Appendix Figure 9), image editing on CelebA-HQ (Figure 6), and latent mixing (Appendix Figure 10).


Q5. "How is the FID of reconstructions computed exactly? Is the reconstructed set of (how many?) samples compared against the set of the original samples?"

A5. Thank you for the suggestion. We will update the manuscript to reflect the details for computing FID.


Q6. "What do you mean by using ProgressiveGAN for the 128x128 architecture in 5.1? Do you mean you just use their 128x128 structure in a static manner, and not the progressive growing?"

A6. We apply progressive growing until we reach 128x128 resolution. Our updated results in the revised version for CelebA-HQ are of size 512x512, still based on ProgressiveGAN. This demonstrates the effectiveness of our DC-VAE being general and not limited to particular VAE architectural designs, attaining high-quality images across different image resolutions.


Q7. "Can you show also latent interpolations or Perceptual Path Length (Karras et al., 2018) measurements?"

A7. Thank you for the suggestion. We compare the PPL score of the DC-VAE Decoder with the ProGAN backbone on CelebA-HQ (Table 6). Our method outperforms StyleALAE (which used StyleGAN backbone) and ProGAN and in terms of PPL metric.

content.title: The paper proposes DC-VAE, a modification of VAE/GAN model that uses contrastive learning to achieve improved perceptual quality in reconstructions and synthesized images, and meaningful semantic representations with respect to downstream classification tasks (MNIST only). Analysis experiments could have been more insightful.
content.review:
The paper presents a novel approach to VAE based generative models, and claims to address the three tasks of reconstruction, synthesis and learning semantic representations. The primary contribution is a novel loss that combines a contrastive loss at the instance level, which assists more faithful reconstructions, with a GAN loss to introduce set-level fidelity, which assists the synthesis quality. Additionally, a multi-scale contrastive learning loss is also used by imposing losses across different layers of the network, as well as at different patches (receptive field sizes). This dual "contradistinctive" loss is well-motivated and appears to work well for datasets like CIFAR-10, STL-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ and LSUN bedroom. The quantitative analysis is done using Inception Score (IS) and Frechet Inception Distance (FID), Pixel Distance, and Perceptual Distance. The paper shows good results on these datasets and settings. 

Strengths
+ Quality of reconstructions and synthesis is very good, and better than state-of-the-art (Intro-VAE). The quantitative analysis is consistent with the qualitative superiority of the proposed method. 
+ The use of contrastive loss together with a GAN based loss is an interesting idea, and it seems to work well based on the qualitative and quantitative results. 

Weaknesses
- Why is h(x,y) in Eq. (6) used as the cosine distance? Would changing it to L_1/L_2 distance help reconstruction better? The cosine similarity is probably appropriate in (He et al., 2020) because of their downstream task of classification, and not reconstruction. What is the impact of changing this critic function on reconstruction? 

- How is the number of negative samples determined for contrastive learning? Why is it 8096, and how do the results change if this number is reduced or increased. An analysis experiment around this could help understand the impact of the contrastive loss. 

- Does the stability of GAN training get impacted by the contrastive learning loss? Particularly, if the parameters like number of negative samples are changed? 

- The paper does not provide details about the training infrastructure used for training this model. It could be helpful to provide these details along with training time, etc. 

- Representation learning experiments are only done on MNIST. Conducting them on CIFAR-10 and/or STL-10 would add more value to the paper. MNIST not having been used elsewhere seems odd and gives the (possibly incorrect) impression that representation learning performance is not good for other datasets. 


Other (minor) issues 
- Please define i (index of anchor point?), and x_j (samples that are not x_i?) in Eq. (6). Please define D_l in the critic function definition that follows. The sentence before Eq. (6) also needs attention, as it refers to a minimization problem, which is not indicated in Eq. (6)
- It seems the second last para before Sec. 4.1 has the Eq. numbers mixed up. It may be worth verifying. 

The results obtained are impressive, however, not all claims are satisfied thoroughly, e.g., the representation learning experiments are weaker as they are only shown on the MNIST dataset. The analysis experiments are limited and do not entirely provide the view of the hyperparameter choices. These are the primary reasons for me to recommend marginally above acceptance threshold. 

I request the authors to comment on the following: 
It will be helpful to understand the implications of the combination of contrastive loss and GAN based losses on the training. 
It will also be helpful to comment on the choice of the critic function. 
Should we expect similar results of representation learning on datasets other than MNIST as well?
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: We thank reviewer 4 for the constructive comments. Please see our answers to the questions below.
content.comment:
Q1. “Why is h(x,y) in Eq. (6) used as the cosine distance? Would changing it to L_1/L_2 distance help reconstruction better? The cosine similarity is probably appropriate in (He et al., 2020) because of their downstream task of classification, and not reconstruction. What is the impact of changing this critic function on reconstruction?”

A1. Intuitively, L1/L2 distance is not a good metric, because the sparsity of high dimension embedding space. I.e. the embedding of every image is far away, and L1/L2 distance will be not informative. Empirically, we find that L2 distance is sensitive to the temperature of the contrastive objective, introducing instability into the training process. We have also tried learnable temperature and feature scaling for L2 distance, but the result was always worse than that of cosine distance.


Q2. “How is the number of negative samples determined for contrastive learning? Why is it 8096, and how do the results change if this number is reduced or increased. An analysis experiment around this could help understand the impact of the contrastive loss.”

A2. Thank you for the comment. We have conducted an experiment to measure the pixel reconstruction error on the test set while varying the number of negative samples. We see that adding the negative samples improves the correspondence between the input image and the reconstructed. For all of our experiments we choose 8096 as the number of negative samples because of memory constraints. Please refer to appendix section A.3 and Figure 11.


Q3. “Does the stability of GAN training get impacted by the contrastive learning loss? Particularly, if the parameters like number of negative samples are changed?”

A3. While running our experiments we do not observe any instability in the GAN training because of the contrastive learning loss. Furthermore, in appendix section A.3 Figure 11 we show that even when we vary the number of negative samples, the training is very stable. For various negative samples from 128 to 8096, the pixel reconstruction error does not diverge versus the training epoch, which implies that there is no training failure. 


Q4. “The paper does not provide details about the training infrastructure used for training this model. It could be helpful to provide these details along with training time, etc.”

A4. Thank you for pointing it out. More details about the training infrastructure will be provided in Appendix.


Q5. “Representation learning experiments are only done on MNIST. Conducting them on CIFAR-10 and/or STL-10 would add more value to the paper. MNIST not having been used elsewhere seems odd and gives the (possibly incorrect) impression that representation learning performance is not good for other datasets.”

A5. For VAE paper have been focusing on the quality of image synthesis, very few, if any, have reported results on representation learning; on the contrast, representation learning papers based on disentanglement learning haven’t typically show synthesis in the general generative model sense to compare with SOTA GAN models. 
We follow the procedure from Guided-VAE used for MNIST. 
To show that DC-VAE learns good representation on other datasets as well. We added image editing results on CelebAHQ (figure 
6), latent space interpolation results on CelebAHQ (figure 5, 9) and LSUN (figure 5), latent mixing results on CelebAHQ (figure 10). 


Q6. Please define i (index of anchor point?), and x_j (samples that are not x_i?) in Eq. (6). Please define D_l in the critic function definition that follows. The sentence before Eq. (6) also needs attention, as it refers to a minimization problem, which is not indicated in Eq. (6)

A6. Thank you for pointing it out. We have revised the definitions regarding Eq. (6).


Q7. It seems the second last para before Sec. 4.1 has the Eq. numbers mixed up. It may be worth verifying.

A7. Thank you for pointing it out. We have revised the references.

content.title: This paper could be considered as a VAE-GAN with a contrastive loss function
content.review:
This paper introduces a discriminator into the VAE framework. The original reconstruction loss is replaced by a adversarial loss and a contrastive loss upon features extracted by the discriminator. The author highlights the ability of reconstruction and generation ability compared with both VAE and GANs. Experimental results show that the proposed DC-VAE outperforms other auto-encoder-based generation methods and obtains comparable results with adversarial generative method. 

Pros,
1. Experimental results seem good.

2. This paper is well-written and easy to read.

3. The source code is provided to make the results reproducible.

Cons,
1. Although a discriminator is introduced into DC-VAE, generation results are worse than GANs on most datasets. Considering that an encoder is also used in DC-VAE but not in GANs, these results seem to be less competitive. 

2. The contrastive loss is interesting, however, no experiment shows results obtained with  contrastive loss only. An ablation study is welcome.

3. In experimental parts, some interesting generative models are missing, such as relativistic GAN [1], PUGAN [2], NVAE

[1] "The relativistic discriminator: a key element missing from standard GAN." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.

[2] "On Positive-Unlabeled Classification in GAN." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2020.

[3] "Nvae: A deep hierarchical variational autoencoder." arXiv preprint arXiv:2007.03898 (2020).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

replying_to: Replying to This paper could be considered as a VAE-GAN with a contrastive loss function
display_title: We thank reviewer 1 for the valuable comments. Please see our answers to the questions below.

content.title: We thank reviewer 1 for the valuable comments. Please see our answers to the questions below.
content.comment:
Q1. “Although a discriminator is introduced into DC-VAE, generation results are worse than GANs on most datasets. Considering that an encoder is also used in DC-VAE but not in GANs, these results seem to be less competitive.”

A1. Thank you for pointing it out but there might be a misunderstanding. The scope of VAE (with both an encoder and decoder) is greater than that of GAN (decoder only) since in addition to sampling/synthesis, VAE can perform reconstruction, classification, and representation learning that are not included in GAN.
In some modeling cases, having an extra module (e.g. making CNN deeper or wider) might be considered as an additional benefit that is expected to enhance the performance. This, however, is not true between VAE and GAN since the encoder module in VAE comes with greater scope of capabilities that GAN doesn't have.

Ideally, we would have hoped the sampling quality of VAE to outperform/match that of GAN while enjoying VAE’s additional encoding capability. Unfortunately, a gap in the synthesis still exists between VAE and GAN. Here we aim to reduce such a gap by introducing a new loss without making architectural changes to the VAE framework. In the experiments, we obtained a significant improvement in the quality of reconstruction and synthesis for the proposed DC-VAE over existing VAEs, nearing the performance of GAN while having the reconstruction and representation learning capabilities that GAN doesn’t have. After training, if only synthesis/sampling is needed, then the encoder in VAE can be removed


Q2. “The contrastive loss is interesting, however, no experiment shows results obtained with contrastive loss only. An ablation study is welcome.”

A2. This is a good point. Indeed, in Figure 4 (row 3) of the original paper, we have already shown an ablation study where results with contrastive loss without the GAN term have been demonstrated. As expected, the reconstruction and synthesis are not satisfactory. This is due to the fact that the contrastive loss alone only makes the construction sufficiently “close to” the input instance discriminatively in the feature space compared with the other instances, but not necessarily to require the construction to be faithful to image manifold. In the original paper, we describe it in Section 5.2 and additionally showed a comparison in network design in Appendix, Figure 7. 


Q3. “In experimental parts, some interesting generative models are missing, such as relativistic GAN [1], PUGAN [2], NVAE”

A3. Thank you for pointing them out. We have added these to the manuscript (Table 2). Our method shows better results than these methods in terms of sampling FID. NVAE focuses on the architectural change for the VAE network; PUGAN and RaGAN focus on stabilizing GAN training. Our approach is orthogonal and can potentially be combined with them.
